newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan seeks $1.2 bln Paris Club debt rescheduling.
newsitem.headline: Jordan seeks $1.2 bln Paris Club debt rescheduling.

text.p: Jordan hopes to conclude a deal this week with the Paris Club of official creditors to reschedule around $1.2 billion of its $6.5 billion foreign debt to push ahead economic reforms, officials said on Sunday.

They said the talks with the Paris Club due to start next Thursday were the fourth such rescheduling rounds since a 1989 economic crisis when the International Monetary Fund intervened after the kingdom failed to service $8 billion of foreign debt.

The deal would reschedule interest payments due between June and early 1999. It should help Jordan reduce its debt repayment burden, currently around $500 million annually, to ensure its IMF-directed economic reforms proceed speedily.

The last major accord in June 1994 rescheduled a similar $1.2 billion of the kingdom's debts over 20 years, including 10 years' grace period. A more limited one last October rescheduled debt worth a total of $308 million slated for repayment between July 1996 and May 1997.
According to official figures, Jordan's total debt stood at $6.5 billion at the end of 1996, nearly half of which was bilateral debt to sovereign creditors.

Jordan hopes its record so far in pursuing an IMF-directed economic restructuring programme will provide it with a sympathetic hearing from official creditors who have expressed confidence in its pace and scope of free-market reforms.

Jordan will argue to the Paris Club that it has gone a long way in meeting IMF targets and deserves favourable terms to ensure it can comfortably surmount major political and social hurdles anticipated as it undertakes advanced economic reforms.
Jordan will begin a new three-year IMF-guided programme next year expected to focus on accelerating the pace of economic structural reforms including rapid privatisation.

But officials privately say the country is not likely to get support for any outright debt forgiveness although they believe creditors are looking favourably at writing off debt in return for investment commitments.
Jordan's implementation of a tough monetary and fiscal stabilisation since 1990 has brought down its debt to GDP ratio to 90 percent in 1996 from a peak of 203.4 percent in 1991.
